Issued at 200 PM CDT Sun Oct 11 2026

Early this afternoon water vapor satellite imagery along with upper 
air anaylisis showed The phasing of a southern stream upper trough 
with the northern stream upper trough across the western US. An 
upper level ridge was located from eastern TX, northward along the 
KS/MO border, north-northeast into IA. The now extra tropical upper 
trough, the remnants from hurricane Isaias, was lifting northeast 
across eastern KY, eastern TN, and north central GA. 

The 17Z surface observations showed a cold front extending from 
northern MN, southwest across eastern SD, then southwestward into 
southwest NE and northeast CO. Across eastern KS, southerly winds 
were increasing to 15 to 20 MPH with some gusts of 25 to 30 MPH. 
Temperatures were in the upper 70s to lower 80s.

Today through Monday:

The upper trough along the western US coast will dig southeast into 
western NV and extend southeast into northwest Mexico. The H5 ridge 
axis across the western Gulf will amplify northward across the mid MS
River Valley. A lee surface trough across the central high Plains 
will deepen in response to strong southwesterly mid level flow across
the central Rockies. The southerly winds will warm afternoon high 
temperatures into the lower 90s. The highs may be near or tie record 
highs for Monday. There will be scattered high thin clouds.

Monday night through Tuesday night:

A southwesterly LLJ of 40-45 KTS will increase through the late 
evening and overnight hours. The HRRR and RAP models show elevated 
showers developing through the early morning hours of Tuesday across
northeast KS in response to the transport of richer moisture 
northward by the LLJ.

The H5 trough will slowly push east into UT and extend 
southward across AZ. The southwesterly H5 flow will increase to 30 
to 40 KTS across the CWA, with the H5 jet max across western KS of 
50-55 KTS. The surface front across NE will move southeast into the 
northern counties of the CWA during the morning hours of Tuesday. 
The NAM12 pushes the front southeast to I-35 by 00Z WED. While the 
GFS and ECMWF show the front becoming stationary across the 
northern counties of the CWA Tuesday afternoon. The NAM12 develops 
1500-2000 J/KG of MLCAPE ahead of the front during the late afternoon
hours. While the GFS/ECMWF only shows 1000-1200 J/KG of MLCAPE. 
However, as the front approaches, thunderstorms will develop due to 
surface convergence and ascent ahead of the H5 jet max. The storms 
may be severe given 40 to 50 KTS of effective shear. Even if the 
NAM12 instability is a bit over done, the low-level veering wind 
profile and curved hodograph show the potential for supercell 
thunderstorms. There will be a stronger EML over spreading the CWA, 
which may limit the coverage of thunderstorms. Any supercell 
thunderstorm may produce all hazards. There remains uncertainties 
based on the location of the front Tuesday afternoon and the strength
of the CAP, but eventually the convergence along the front should 
cause scattered to numerous thunderstorms to develop during the
evening hours. Some of the storms may be severe ahead of the front 
into the evening hours. 

There remains much uncertainty on where the front may become 
stationary overnight. The NAM12 moves the front south of the CWA to 
the KS/OK border after midnight. While the GFS and ECMWF show the 
front becoming stationary along the southeast counties of the CWA. 
Strong isentropic lift over the front will cause showers and 
elevated thunderstorms to continue through the early morning hours 
of Wednesday. 

Wednesday through Thursday:

The extended range models are in better agreement. The GFS lifts the 
upper low over the Four Corners region northeast across north 
central NE by 18Z WED, which begins to phase with an H5 trough 
digging southeast out of central Canada into the Upper Midwest. The 
ECMWF shears apart the upper low over the Four Corners region, while 
an amplified H5 trough digs southeast out central canada into the 
upper Midwest by 00Z FRI.

There remains some uncertainty on where the frontal boundary will be 
located. The GFS shows the boundary remaining stationary across the 
far southeast counties, which would keep most surface based storms to 
our south. The ECMWF shows the front slowly shifting north Wednesday
night into Thursday morning. Both extended range models show a 
strong front pushing southeast across the CWA on Thursday, as strong
low-level CAA develops across the northern and central plains to the
west of an amplifying H5 trough across the Upper Midwest.

Isentropic lift with richer 850mb moisture advection will cause 
showers and elevated thunderstorms Wednesday into Thursday morning.
